lesson.title: Measuring Phase: Comparing Two Signals on One Clock
lesson.summary: Phase measurement compares the timing of two same frequency waveforms displayed together on an oscilloscope, converting the horizontal shift between corresponding points on each trace into a phase angle.
lesson.body:
Phase angle describes how far one periodic waveform is shifted in time relative to another of the same frequency, expressed not in seconds but as a fraction of a full cycle, in degrees, where a full cycle is 360 degrees. To measure it in practice, you need two signals displayed on a shared time axis at once, which is exactly what a two channel oscilloscope gives you: connect one signal, say the input to a circuit, to channel one, and the related signal, the circuit's output, to channel two, and both traces are drawn against the same horizontal time scale.

With both waveforms on screen, you pick a feature that repeats clearly on each one, most often the rising zero crossing, the point where the voltage crosses zero heading upward, and measure how many divisions separate that feature on channel one from the same feature on channel two. Multiply that division count by the time/div setting the same way you would to measure a period, and you get a time shift, delta t, between the two signals. To convert that time shift into a phase angle, you compare it to the shared period T of both waveforms, since you already know how to measure that from either trace: phase angle = (delta t / T) times 360 degrees.

Here is a worked example. Both waveforms have a period of 10 ms, the same 100 Hz signal from earlier examples. Channel two's rising zero crossing occurs 2.5 ms after channel one's rising zero crossing. The phase angle is (2.5 ms / 10 ms) times 360 degrees = 90 degrees, meaning the channel two signal lags a quarter cycle behind channel one. This kind of measurement is exactly how you would characterize the delay a filter or reactive circuit introduces between its input and output, and it depends entirely on the oscilloscope's ability to hold both traces stable and synchronized against the same time axis, which is the job of triggering.
